title.narrative: NIHR Global Health Research Development Awards: NIHR208273 - Development of a research partnership for improving monitoring and treatment of neonatal infections in Bangladesh

description.narrative:
The Bangladesh Initiative for Advancing Research on Neonatal Infections (BARN) was supported through the NIHR Global Health Research Development Award (Phase I) with the overarching aim of establishing a sustainable, equitable research partnership to address the persistent burden of neonatal infections in Bangladesh. Neonatal sepsis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs. The Development Award was designed to strengthen locally led research capacity, improve infection monitoring, and generate the partnerships, preliminary data, and translational pathways needed to develop a competitive, researcher-led global health proposal.
Led by the Child Health Research Foundation (CHRF) in Bangladesh in partnership with the UK Hub of the Centres for Antimicrobial Optimisation Network (CAMO-Net), the award prioritised equitable collaboration, Southâ€“North knowledge exchange, and meaningful engagement with clinicians, communities, and policymakers. Activities were structured across five interlinked work packages encompassing partnership development, epidemiological research, translational technology development, computational modelling, and research capacity strengthening. Rather than discrete outputs alone, the award emphasised process-oriented outcomes, building trust, shared ownership, and long-term collaboration, reflecting the intent of the Development Awards programme.
The most significant achievement of the award was the establishment of a functional and durable Southâ€“North research partnership, with CHRF as the scientific and administrative lead. This partnership was operationalised through regular scientific meetings, reciprocal visits, co-led workshops, and joint engagement with international stakeholders and funders. Importantly, decision-making, agenda-setting, and data ownership were based in Bangladesh, contributing to more balanced power dynamics and strengthening local leadership. As a direct result of this partnership, the team co-developed multiple follow-on research concepts and funding plans, including proposals focused on improved microbiological diagnostics, AMR transmission modelling, and host biomarker-based infection monitoring methods for tackling neonatal sepsis.
The award enabled several strands of research activity that would not have been feasible without Development Award support. Retrospective analyses of neonatal sepsis data across four large paediatric hospitals in Bangladesh provided new insights into temporal trends in pathogen distribution, the rising burden of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative organisms, and persistently high mortality rates among infected neonates. These analyses highlighted substantial diagnostic gaps, including a large proportion of infections that remain uncharacterised using current routine microbiological methods in LMIC settings. In parallel, the partnership supported the development of computational models to investigate the transmission of drug-resistant organisms within neonatal units, leveraging routinely collected clinical and microbiological data. This work led to the creation of a novel analytical pipeline, termed PathoPATH, for infection tracking and hotspot identification, laying the foundation for future hospital-based intervention studies.
The award also supported early-stage translational research through engagement with engineers and clinicians on the adaptation of microneedle-based biosensors for neonatal care. Through clinician meetings, patient and public involvement (PPI) activities, and technology demonstrations, the project gathered critical feedback on feasibility, usability, and clinical relevance, informing future design and validation studies. While not intended to deliver deployable technologies within Phase I, this work established a clear translational pathway aligned with local clinical priorities.
Research capacity strengthening was a core outcome of the award. Through targeted training in data science, research methods and ethics, the project enhanced individual and institutional capacity at CHRF. Early-career researchers benefited from mentorship, international exposure, and leadership opportunities, including successful applications for independent fellowships and travel awards. These gains extend beyond the life of the award and contribute to a growing ecosystem of locally led neonatal infection research in Bangladesh.
In summary, the BARN Development Award delivered substantial value by strengthening equitable research partnerships, generating critical preliminary data, building local research capacity, and positioning a Bangladesh-led consortium to compete for major global health funding. The award demonstrates how targeted Development Awards can catalyse long-term impact by investing in people, partnerships, and processes, even in complex and uncertain contexts.
